body:
> I can't claim understanding of this change by way of understanding when exactly a deeply nested element is presented by my screen reader and how (though who can, really, other than someone who develops screen readers and not games) but I can say that, with this patch in place, I can consistently tab off and onto trees and hear the correct value spoken by Orca.

This is a clear violation of our contribution guidelines, see [here](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/pull_requests/pull_request_guidelines.html#ai-assisted-contributions) and [here](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/pull_requests/pull_request_guidelines.html#contribute-only-what-you-understand) I would say

I don't think this is a valid contribution

Do what you want with it.

Look, I get it, I hate slop PRs as much as anyone else. But if your bar for submissions is that I have to deeply understand precisely how my screen reader presents a deeply-nested row in a tree, that a small self-contained change is not exempt, and that lived/tested experience doesn't matter, then you're never going to truly fix some of these accessibility issues. The overlap of folks with that understanding isn't fixing game engines. They're buried deep in some screen reader project, or in some company's accessibility team working on enterprise software. And they're probably not volunteering their off-time to do it either because it's exhausting AF. I appreciate the work that's been done, but if all you do is shut people down because they don't understand every single nuance of the accessibility stack, then this is as good as your access is ever going to get, full stop.

I haven't tested this with multiple cells. It's possible it might fall down there and needs some work. In my defense, the scene tree is the only tree example I've ever used in Godot, it's not particularly accessible, and to me "inaccessible" and "invisible" are often the same. I'd be open to making this work if someone can point me to a premade tree example with multiple cells, but if the bar for submitting Godot accessibility patches is an intimate understanding of how Orca and NVDA present your bespoke widgets, then count me out.

Anyway, won't argue anymore, it's your project. Though I'd bet that if someone provably fixed a rendering glitch, you wouldn't expect them to have intimate knowledge of the specific hardware, driver, or graphics stack that caused the glitch. You'd accept it as long as they understood the code they submitted, which I do, and as long as it looks good. But hey, this only affects disabled folks, so it's fine, won't matter at all to 99+% of your users.

To be clear I didn't reject this, I just outlined that that description was IMO clearly against our contribution guidelines. Using AI tools to substitute understanding is not appropriate IMO, and that's what the guidelines also hold

Understood. That leaves me in the awkward position of wanting to recommend Godot because you're literally the only accessible engine out there, but being hesitant to do so because of this very high standard. You're essentially asking that contributors to your accessibility stack have an intimate understanding of how every platform accessibility API behaves, and as someone who has done or been adjacent to this work for decades, I can probably count the number of folks with that knowledge on one hand. You're within your rights to do that for sure, but it's worth naming that the accessibility warts you have today won't go away if the only ones who can contribute are those who just innately know how these APIs work under the hood. And if that's how it is, then I need to stop building projects on Godot immediately, because while things are certainly good, vast swaths of the editor are currently unusable, and even the simplest of fixes isn't going to be accepted unless it's submitted by one of a small handful of people alive today. That's untenable when accessibility is a requirement, not just a nice-to-have.

That's not what I'm asking and perhaps there's some miscommunication here, but it sounded like you didn't understand the solution and the PR code, and again you decided to close this yourself I didn't close it or say that it should beyond expressing that my understanding of it was outside of our contribution acceptance

No one said anything about "innately know how these APIs work under the hood", that's a misrepresentation of what I said

To clarify:
* It sounded like you did not understand what you were contributing, and that you needed AI tools to substitute that knowledge
* We require contributors to understand their contributions well enough to adjust them and take responsibility for them

Accessibility is not just a nice-to-have, and that's partially why we don't lower our standards in that area

If my understanding of what your disclaimer means then I am sorry, but that was my at the face value reading of it

OK, fair enough, and apologies for the over-reaction. I thought I had made the limits of my lack of understanding clearer by stating exactly what specifically I didn't understand immediately after the disclosure, and explicitly in the text of mine you quoted. I've literally spent hours this week using Claude to fix accessibility issues in this and other projects I depend on or use so it's a bit exhausting, particularly when I'd rather be doing just about anything else.

I'll reopen this then, and if someone wants to test this with a tree with multiple cells, or create one for me to test with, I'll revise if needed and report back. I don't fully understand the shape of Godot's trees, but only because I can't actually work with them to gain that understanding, which is what accessibility is all about.
Good we could work that misunderstanding out!
